extracted.intended_audience: students and enthusiasts of number theory / discrete mathematics (readers of Gödel's Lost Letter)
extracted.subtask_description: An expository blog post explaining the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic (existence and uniqueness of prime factorization) and giving several concrete examples and historical notes showing how and where unique factorization can fail in other number systems (cyclotomic integers, special subsets of N, quadratic integer rings, polynomial rings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic (FTA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every natural number greater than 1 is the product of primes, and moreover this decomposition is unique up to ordering of the primes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classic theorem central to number theory; existence and uniqueness are the two parts. This is the baseline property whose failure is the subject of the post.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure of unique factorization in other number systems (cyclotomic integers)
rubrics_metrics.description: FTA can fail for other kinds of numbers such as the cyclotomic integers used in attempts to prove Fermat's Last Theorem; Lamé's proof incorrectly assumed unique factorization in these rings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical context: Lamé used numbers generated by the nth roots of unity; Liouville questioned Lamé's assumption about unique factorization; Kummer showed FTA held for some primes but failed for others in these rings. The post notes Kummer replaced FTA with a weaker and very useful statement which allowed his methods to prove FLT in many cases but not all.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hilbert numbers as a counterexample family
rubrics_metrics.description: The set of Hilbert numbers (a specified subset of natural numbers — discussed as the set of integers of a particular congruence class) admits a notion of 'Hilbert primes' and every sufficiently large Hilbert number is a product of Hilbert primes, but factorization need not be unique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post emphasizes that a number can be 'prime' in the subset without being prime among all natural numbers; some Hilbert numbers can be factored in more than one way, so FTA fails for Hilbert numbers. (Commentary later identifies H = {4k+1} as a natural example.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Even positive integers example of non-unique factorization
rubrics_metrics.description: Take E = the set of all even positive integers. E is closed under multiplication and addition; primes in E are described; every element of E is a product of primes in E; yet factorization in E is not unique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete description from the post: a prime in E is of the form 2p where p is an odd natural prime. For distinct odd primes p and q we have a nonunique factorization 2·p·q = (2p)·q = (2q)·p, showing FTA fails in E. The post highlights this as an extremely simple and pedagogically useful counterexample.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-unique factorization in quadratic integer rings Z[√-N]
rubrics_metrics.description: Rings of integers of the form Z[√-N] can fail to have unique factorization; for N > 2 the ring Z[√-N] typically does not have unique factorization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pete Clark's comment in the thread sketches that non-unique factorization in these quadratic rings can be related to representations of primes by binary quadratic forms (x^2+Ny^2) and provides this as a 'real life' example of UFD failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-unique factorization in polynomial/trigonometric rings (R[sinθ,cosθ])
rubrics_metrics.description: The ring R[sin θ, cos θ] of real trigonometric polynomials does not have unique factorization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example given: cos θ · cos θ = (1 + sin θ)·(1 − sin θ), where cos θ, 1+sin θ and 1−sin θ are nonassociate irreducibles, demonstrating non-uniqueness. The post cites a reference (Trotter) for an elementary treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modern algebraic perspective: the setting for unique factorization
rubrics_metrics.description: Unique factorization is naturally studied in commutative, cancellative monoids with an identity element; some ad hoc subsets (like E without 1) are less natural from this abstract perspective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commentary (Pete Clark) points out that the modern viewpoint frames UFDs in the language of commutative cancellative monoids (or integral domains), and that the even-integers example lacks an identity element, making it somewhat contrived though pedagogically simple.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between prime elements and irreducible elements
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a potential confusion between 'prime element' and 'irreducible element' in these contexts; the two notions are not always equivalent in general rings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A commenter flags the confusion and links to explanatory material. (In integral domains, 'prime' implies 'irreducible', but the converse need not hold; being careful about these definitions is important when discussing factorization properties in non-UFD settings.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Kummer's remedy: weakening unique factorization to salvage arithmetic methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Kummer found a weaker but useful replacement for unique factorization (leading toward the theory of ideal/class groups) which allowed progress on Fermat's Last Theorem for many primes even when ordinary unique factorization failed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post notes Kummer's insight as historically significant: instead of ordinary prime factorization in the cyclotomic integers one works with a modified algebraic apparatus that compensates for failure of unique factorization (the post does not give full technical details).
